title: Five Spooky Sky Targets to Spot This Halloween Season
summary: Halloween is a perfect excuse to look up, because the autumn sky is full of myths and bright surprises. You do not need a telescope for these five targets, just a dark sky and patience. Start with the Pleiades, a tight cluster that looks like six or seven bright stars to the naked eye. Binoculars reveal dozens more from a cluster of about 1,000 stars. Ancient Celtic druids celebrated Samhain, a forerunner of Halloween, when the Pleiades reached its highest point at midnight in autumn, a time when people once believed the veil between the living and the dead was thinnest. From the United States, find the three stars of Orion's Belt before midnight, follow an imaginary line upward to the bright orange star Aldebaran, then look a little higher. Next, meet Algol, nicknamed the Demon Star, an eye of the Gorgon Medusa in the constellation Perseus. Algol is really two stars orbiting each other. Every 2.867 days, one star passes in front of the other, making Algol look about 3.3 times dimmer during a 10-hour eclipse. It will not be eclipsed on Halloween night in 2026, but dimming may be visible around October 29 and November 1. Then look southeast after sunset for Cetus, the sea monster or whale, whose circlet of stars shines to the right of the Pleiades. Around the full moon on October 26, look for bright, spiderweb-like streaks around the Moon craters Tycho, Copernicus, and Kepler. They are bright material thrown out by the impacts that made those young craters, best seen at full moon. Finally, watch for the Taurid meteors, bright and slow-moving, seeming to streak away from a patch of sky near the Pleiades in Taurus. They take patience and luck, but one long fireball can make the night feel magical.
why_it_matters: Knowing what to look for turns an ordinary autumn night into a chance to see real stars, myths, and meteors with your own eyes.

background_read: A constellation is a group of stars that people long ago joined into a picture, such as a hero or a sea monster, and many of these pictures come from old myths.
A star cluster is a group of stars born close together and still travelling together through space.
Meteors are streaks of light made when small bits of space dust burn up in Earth's air, and they can look brightest on dark, clear nights.
The bright streaks around some Moon craters are material thrown out when space rocks crashed into the Moon long ago.
